patient.name: Chantelle Brooks
patient.complaint: Gritty, staring eyes and double vision when looking up
background: Graves' disease diagnosed 4 months ago, on carbimazole

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely finding' in a woman with Graves' and gritty, prominent eyes, plus questions on smoking, radioiodine and sight-threatening red flags (reduced colour vision, RAPD).

points: Eyes feel **gritty**, watery and sore in bright light.
Friends say she looks like she is **staring**.
Double vision when she looks up at the salon shelves.
Pressure behind both eyes in the mornings.

steps.lead: Chantelle's eye symptoms are not a separate eye disease: they are the **orbital** arm of her Graves' autoimmunity.
Chantelle is a woman with Graves' who **smokes 15 a day**: smoking is the biggest modifiable driver of worse eye disease.
Grittiness, photophobia, diplopia, retro-orbital pressure and prominent eyes: Chantelle has the textbook symptom list.

points: **White sclera visible above both irises** in primary gaze.
Upper lids lag behind the eye as she looks down.
Both eyes protrude; red, swollen conjunctivae and puffy lids.
Upgaze restricted, with **diplopia**; pupils normal, acuity 6/6.

steps.lead: The sclera above Chantelle's iris is **Dalrymple's sign**; the lag on down gaze is **Von Graefe's sign**; the protrusion is **proptosis**.

steps.q: Which sign is specific to Graves' rather than any cause of thyrotoxicosis?
steps.r: **Proptosis** (with restricted eye movements) comes from orbital autoimmunity, so it means Graves'. Lid lag and lid retraction can occur in any thyrotoxicosis from sympathetic overactivity.

steps.lead: Chantelle's proptosis and lid retraction leave her cornea exposed, so **exposure keratopathy** is her most likely complication.
Chantelle's acuity is 6/6 and pupils are normal today. Any fall in **acuity or colour vision**, or an **RAPD**, would make this sight-threatening.

steps.text: Lid lag alone does not mean thyroid eye disease: it can be sympathetic overactivity in any thyrotoxicosis. **Proptosis, diplopia and soft-tissue swelling** mean orbital disease.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (TFTs) and, with an RAPD or reduced colour vision, 'urgent CT or MRI of the orbits' showing enlarged extraocular muscles.

steps.q: What confirms Chantelle's thyroid eye disease?
o: Clinical assessment with thyroid function tests
steps.r: TED is a **clinical diagnosis** backed by thyroid function. Imaging is reserved for red flags or diagnostic doubt.

steps.lead: No single test proves Chantelle's TED. Her **signs plus Graves' blood results** make the diagnosis.

steps.title: Chantelle's thyroid bloods
steps.text: Still thyrotoxic on carbimazole, and TRAb positive: the same antibodies drive her eye disease.

steps.lead: Chantelle's **low TSH, high T4** is the thyrotoxic pattern of Graves'. Her eye disease can run its own course even as TFTs normalise.

visual.title: Proptosis (Hertel exophthalmometry)
visual.label: Chantelle 23 mm
visual.caption: Measures how far the cornea sits in front of the lateral orbital rim. Above about 20 mm is proptosis.

steps.text: Measuring proptosis gives a baseline to track at every visit.

points: Six weeks later: colours look **washed out** in her left eye.

steps.lead: Chantelle's RAPD means the optic nerve is being squeezed. She needs **urgent CT or MRI orbits**, which shows **enlarged extraocular muscles** crowding the orbital apex.

steps.text: In TED the **inferior and medial recti** are usually the first enlarged muscles, so **upgaze** is restricted first.

management.exam: Expect 'most appropriate initial management' for mild disease (lubricants, smoking cessation, control thyroid), active moderate-to-severe disease (IV corticosteroids), and sight-threatening disease (urgent ophthalmology, IV steroids, orbital decompression).

steps.q: Chantelle's acuity is 6/6 today. Which first step helps her gritty eyes most?
steps.r: **Lubricants** are first-line supportive treatment for exposure and dryness. Surgery is for sight-threatening disease.

steps.lead: Chantelle gets **lubricants**, carbimazole and a beta-blocker for her thyrotoxic symptoms, and firm **smoking cessation** advice.

steps.text: **Radioactive iodine** can worsen eye disease. In a smoker with active TED it is avoided, or given only under steroid cover.

visual.title: Clinical Activity Score (CAS)
visual.label: Chantelle 5
visual.caption: Points for pain, redness and swelling. Active moderate-to-severe disease is what IV steroids treat.

steps.text: Activity score helps decide who needs immunosuppression.

steps.lead: Chantelle's disease is **active and moderate-to-severe** (CAS 5, diplopia, proptosis), so she is offered **IV corticosteroids**.

steps.title: Stepping up thyroid eye disease
nodes: Mild: lubricants, stop smoking, control thyroid
steps.caption: Reduced acuity or colour vision, disc changes or corneal ulceration jump straight to the emergency arm.

steps.q: Chantelle now has a left RAPD and acuity 6/18. What is needed?
o: Increase carbimazole and review in 6 weeks
Urgent ophthalmology review and IV steroids
steps.r: Compressive optic neuropathy is **sight-threatening**: same-day ophthalmology and **IV steroids**, with decompression if vision does not recover.

steps.lead: Chantelle's vision does not improve after IV steroids, so she has **urgent orbital decompression** to relieve pressure on the optic nerve.

visual.title: Chantelle's left eye
visual.caption: Vision fell with optic nerve compression, stayed down on steroids and recovered after decompression.

steps.lead: Chantelle's care follows **EUGOGO** principles: stop smoking, restore euthyroidism, treat by activity and severity, and act fast on sight-threatening disease.

science.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely mechanism...?' for proptosis (TSH receptor antibodies stimulating orbital fibroblasts), diplopia (restrictive myopathy), or why smoking and radioiodine worsen the disease.

steps.lead: Chantelle's orbital fibroblasts carry the **same TSH receptor** as her thyroid cells, so the Graves' antibodies attack both.

steps.title: From antibody to proptosis
nodes: Muscle and fat swell with oedema
Fixed bony orbit: eye pushed forward
steps.caption: The bony orbit cannot expand, so swelling has only one way to go: forwards and backwards onto the nerve.

steps.lead: Chantelle's proptosis, puffy lids and later optic nerve compression all come from **swollen muscle and fat in a fixed box**.

steps.q: Why does Chantelle have double vision on upgaze?
o: Myasthenic fatigue of the eye muscles
Restrictive myopathy of the extraocular muscles
steps.r: Swollen, fibrosed muscles cannot stretch, so the eye is **tethered**: a restrictive, not neurological, problem.

steps.lead: Chantelle's inferior rectus is swollen and stiff, so it cannot relax to let her eye look up: **restrictive myopathy**.
Chantelle's 15 a day add **oxidative stress and cytokines** to the orbit, making her disease more severe and less responsive.
Radioiodine would kill thyroid cells, release antigen and push Chantelle's **TRAb levels up**, fuelling her orbital inflammation.

o: Lid retraction showing the superior limbus
Loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows
mcq.r: Dalrymple's sign is lid retraction exposing sclera above the iris (superior limbus).
Von Graefe's sign is the upper lid lagging behind the eye on down gaze.

mcq.q: What is the most common complication of thyroid eye disease?
mcq.r: Exposure keratopathy from inadequate corneal coverage is most common.

mcq.q: Which modifiable risk factor most worsens thyroid eye disease?
mcq.r: Smoking accelerates and worsens disease; advise cessation.

mcq.q: Which sign means urgent CT or MRI of the orbits is needed?
mcq.r: An RAPD suggests compressive optic neuropathy: urgent orbital imaging.

mcq.q: What does orbital CT or MRI typically show in thyroid eye disease?
mcq.r: Swollen extraocular muscles are the classic imaging finding.

mcq.q: What is the first-line supportive treatment for mild thyroid eye disease?
mcq.r: Lubricants, plus smoking cessation and control of the thyroid.

mcq.q: Which thyroid treatment can worsen thyroid eye disease?
mcq.r: Radioiodine can transiently raise TRAb levels and flare eye disease.

mcq.q: What is needed for sight-threatening compressive optic neuropathy that fails IV steroids?
mcq.r: Urgent surgical orbital decompression relieves pressure on the optic nerve.

mcq.q: Which cells in the orbit are targeted in thyroid eye disease?
mcq.r: Orbital fibroblasts express the TSH receptor and are activated by TRAb.

technique.stem: A 42 year old woman has a 3 month history of gritty, watery eyes and a feeling of pressure behind them. She has lost 6 kg and feels hot all the time. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 132/70 mmHg. Both eyes protrude, with sclera visible above the irises, and she has diplopia on looking up.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: is this an eye problem or a systemic one showing in the eye?

clues: lost 6 kg and feels hot all the time
steps.x: Thyrotoxic symptoms plus bilateral proptosis, lid retraction and restricted upgaze, in a smoker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Graves' disease with **thyroid eye disease**.

elim: Allergic conjunctivitis itches and does not cause proptosis or diplopia.
Myasthenia causes fatigable ptosis, the opposite of lid retraction.
Orbital cellulitis is acute, unilateral and febrile.
Lymphoma is usually unilateral and has no thyrotoxic features.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid eye disease.** Bilateral proptosis + lid retraction + thyrotoxic = Graves' orbitopathy.

technique.stem: A 35 year old woman has a 2 month history of prominent, gritty eyes. Her partner says she looks like she is staring. She has no known medical problems. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 126/74 mmHg. She has bilateral lid retraction and mild proptosis. Visual acuity and colour vision are normal and there is no RAPD.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation: the first and simplest test that fits.

clues: bilateral lid retraction and mild proptosis
steps.x: Suspected Graves' eye disease with no sight-threatening features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thyroid function tests**: expect low TSH, high T4.

elim: CT orbits is for an RAPD or sight-threatening signs, which she does not have.
MRI brain does not assess the thyroid or orbit.
Evoked potentials are for demyelination, not TED.
Visual fields do not identify the cause; she needs her thyroid status first.

steps.x: **C. Thyroid function tests.** Clinical diagnosis + TFTs; image only for red flags.

technique.stem: A 40 year old woman has Graves' disease treated with carbimazole. She has mild thyroid eye disease with gritty eyes and minimal proptosis. Visual acuity and colour vision are normal. She smokes 25 cigarettes a day. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which intervention will most reduce her risk of worsening eye disease?

steps.x: It asks what reduces progression, not what soothes symptoms.

clues: Visual acuity and colour vision are normal
steps.x: Mild disease in a heavy smoker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stop smoking**: the biggest modifiable risk factor.

elim: There is no infection.
Decompression is for sight-threatening disease.
Radioiodine can worsen eye disease, especially in smokers.
Antihistamines treat allergy, not TED.

steps.x: **D. Smoking cessation.** Lubricants for symptoms, stopping smoking for progression.

technique.stem: A 46 year old woman with Graves' disease and mild eye symptoms had radioactive iodine 6 weeks ago. Her eyes are now more painful, red and swollen, and she has new double vision. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. She has worsening proptosis.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for the worsening of her eye disease?
o: Direct radiation injury to the orbit
Hypothyroidism causing myxoedema of the orbit
Rise in TSH receptor antibodies after release of thyroid antigen

steps.x: Mechanism: why did treatment make the eyes worse?
A flare of active TED shortly after radioiodine.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dying thyroid cells **release antigen** and **TRAb levels rise**, driving orbital fibroblasts harder.

elim: Radioiodine is taken up by the thyroid, not the orbit.
Hypothyroid myxoedema does not cause active orbital inflammation.
No fever or unilateral signs; this is autoimmune.
Antibodies go up, not down.

steps.x: **E. Rise in TSH receptor antibodies.** Radioiodine releases antigen and boosts TRAb.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman has a 2 month history of dry, gritty eyes that are sensitive to light. She has had palpitations and weight loss. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 130/72 mmHg. Both eyes are red, with periorbital swelling and bilateral proptosis. Eye movements are restricted on upgaze.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Bilateral proptosis, restricted upgaze and a thyrotoxic biochemistry point to Graves' orbitopathy. Orbital cellulitis is unilateral and febrile.

steps.x: Diagnosis of an eye problem in a thyrotoxic patient.
Thyrotoxic, with bilateral proptosis and restrictive myopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thyroid eye disease** (Graves').

elim: Allergy is itchy, without proptosis.
Episcleritis is a localised red patch, no proptosis.
Cellulitis is unilateral with fever.
Sjögren's gives dry eyes and mouth, not proptosis or thyrotoxicosis.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid eye disease.** Bilateral proptosis + thyrotoxicosis.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman with Graves' disease is reviewed in clinic. She complains that her eyes feel prominent and gritty. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. Looking straight ahead, the upper eyelids sit higher than normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her eyes in primary gaze?
practice.e: Lid retraction exposing the superior limbus (Dalrymple's sign) is never seen in a normal eye and is classic for thyroid eye disease. Ptosis is the opposite.

steps.x: Examination finding in primary gaze.

clues: upper eyelids sit higher than normal
steps.x: Lid retraction in Graves'.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dalrymple's sign**: white sclera above the iris.

elim: Ptosis is a low lid; hers are retracted.
Small pupils suggest Horner's or opiates.
Papilloedema reflects raised intracranial pressure.
A fixed dilated pupil suggests a third nerve palsy.

steps.x: **D. Sclera visible above the iris.** Dalrymple's: superior limbus showing.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman has thyroid eye disease with marked proptosis. She cannot fully close her eyes at night. Over the past week her right eye has become more painful and watery, and she is sensitive to light. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. Fluorescein shows punctate staining over the lower cornea.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her worsening eye symptoms?
practice.e: Proptosis with lagophthalmos leaves the lower cornea exposed: exposure keratopathy, the most common complication. Herpes keratitis gives a dendritic ulcer, not inferior punctate staining.

steps.x: Cause of new symptoms: think complication.

clues: cannot fully close her eyes at night
punctate staining over the lower cornea
steps.x: Lagophthalmos and inferior corneal staining: the cornea is drying out.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Exposure keratopathy.**

elim: Uveitis gives a small pupil and ciliary flush, not corneal staining.
Optic neuropathy reduces acuity and colour vision, without corneal staining.
Herpes keratitis shows a dendritic ulcer.
Retinal detachment gives flashes, floaters and a field shadow, not corneal staining.

steps.x: **C. Exposure keratopathy.** Most common TED complication.

practice.stem: A 39 year old woman with Graves' disease had radioactive iodine 5 weeks ago. Before treatment she had mild gritty eyes. She now has painful, swollen eyelids, red eyes and new double vision. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her worsening eye disease?
practice.e: Radioiodine can worsen thyroid eye disease by raising TSH receptor antibodies; her smoking adds to the risk. Cellulitis would be unilateral and febrile.

steps.x: Most likely cause of a flare.
Flare weeks after radioiodine, with rising antibodies, in a smoker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Radioactive iodine** has triggered a flare.

elim: Carbimazole causes rash or agranulocytosis, not orbitopathy.
Cellulitis is unilateral with fever.
Hypothyroidism does not explain a rise in antibodies and acute orbital inflammation.
Viral conjunctivitis does not cause diplopia.

steps.x: **D. Radioactive iodine treatment.** It raises TRAb; avoid it, or give steroid cover, in active TED.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man with active thyroid eye disease says colours look faded in his left eye over 2 weeks. Left visual acuity is 6/24 and right is 6/6. The swinging light test shows a left relative afferent pupillary defect. Both eyes are proptosed. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his visual loss?
practice.e: Reduced acuity and colour vision with an RAPD in active TED means swollen orbital contents are compressing the optic nerve. Exposure keratopathy does not cause an RAPD.

steps.x: Cause of visual loss in a TED patient: is it surface or nerve?
Colour desaturation + RAPD = optic nerve.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Compressive optic neuropathy**: sight-threatening.

elim: CRVO gives sudden loss with a haemorrhagic fundus.
Keratopathy affects the cornea, not the pupil reflex.
GCA comes with headache, jaw claudication and raised ESR, usually over 50 with no TED.
Optic neuritis affects young adults with painful eye movement, without proptosis.

steps.x: **B. Compressive optic neuropathy.** RAPD in TED = emergency.

practice.stem: A 41 year old woman with Graves' disease has double vision when looking upwards. She has bilateral proptosis and lid retraction. Pupils, acuity and colour vision are normal. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her double vision?
o: Restrictive myopathy of the inferior rectus
practice.e: In TED the inferior rectus is commonly enlarged and fibrosed, so it cannot relax to allow elevation: a restrictive myopathy. A third nerve palsy would give ptosis and a 'down and out' eye.

steps.x: Cause of diplopia: nerve, junction or muscle?
TED with restricted upgaze.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Swollen, stiff **inferior rectus**: restrictive myopathy.

elim: INO is a brainstem lesion, typically MS.
Myasthenia causes fatigable ptosis, not lid retraction.
Sixth nerve palsy causes horizontal diplopia with failed abduction.
Third nerve palsy causes ptosis and a down-and-out eye.

steps.x: **C. Restrictive myopathy.** TED diplopia is mechanical, not neurological.

practice.stem: A 48 year old woman with Graves' orbitopathy has reduced colour vision in her right eye. Right visual acuity has dropped from 6/6 to 6/18 over 10 days, and there is a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Repeat thyroid function tests in 6 weeks
Urgent CT or MRI of the orbits
practice.e: An RAPD with falling acuity and colour vision suggests compressive optic neuropathy: urgent orbital imaging shows enlarged extraocular muscles at the apex. Thyroid imaging does not assess the orbit.

steps.x: Which investigation, given red flags.
Sight-threatening optic nerve compression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent CT or MRI orbits.**

elim: Waiting 6 weeks risks permanent visual loss.
Isotope scans assess the gland, not the orbit.
Thyroid ultrasound does not help the eye.
Three months is far too slow for an RAPD.

steps.x: **D. Urgent CT or MRI of the orbits.** RAPD = image now.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has noticed her eyes look more prominent over 3 months. She has had tremor, anxiety and weight loss. She has bilateral lid retraction and mild proptosis with a diffuse goitre. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 134/68 mmHg. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is raised.
practice.q: Which further blood test best confirms the cause of her eye disease?
practice.e: TSH receptor antibodies confirm Graves' disease and are the same antibodies that drive orbital fibroblast activation. TPO antibodies also occur in Hashimoto's and are not specific.

steps.x: A blood test to confirm the autoimmune cause.

clues: bilateral lid retraction and mild proptosis
TSH is suppressed and free T4 is raised
steps.x: Thyrotoxicosis with eye signs: Graves'.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **TSH receptor antibodies.**

elim: Anti-thyroglobulin is non-specific.
Calcitonin is a medullary thyroid cancer marker.
Thyroglobulin is used to follow differentiated thyroid cancer.
TPO antibodies also occur in Hashimoto's.

steps.x: **E. TSH receptor antibodies.** Same antibody, gland and orbit.

practice.stem: A 37 year old woman with Graves' disease, now euthyroid on carbimazole, has gritty, dry eyes worse in the wind. She has minimal proptosis, normal eye movements, normal acuity and normal colour vision. She has stopped smoking. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her eyes?
practice.e: Mild, inactive disease with surface symptoms is treated with lubricants while the thyroid stays controlled and she stays off cigarettes. IV steroids are for active moderate-to-severe disease.

steps.x: Initial management: first grade the severity.
Mild disease, thyroid controlled, already stopped smoking.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lubricating eye drops.**

elim: IV steroids are for active moderate-to-severe disease.
Decompression is for sight-threatening disease.
Radiotherapy is a specialist option for moderate-to-severe disease.
Radioiodine can worsen eye disease.

steps.x: **B. Lubricating eye drops.** Mild TED: lubricate, control thyroid, no smoking.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has Graves' orbitopathy. Over 2 months her eyes have become painful, red and swollen, with worsening proptosis and constant diplopia. Visual acuity and colour vision are normal and there is no RAPD. Her clinical activity score is 5 out of 7. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Active, moderate-to-severe disease without optic neuropathy is treated with IV corticosteroids. Decompression is reserved for sight-threatening disease not responding to steroids.

steps.x: Management by activity and severity.

clues: clinical activity score is 5 out of 7
steps.x: Active (CAS 5) and moderate-to-severe, but not sight-threatening.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV corticosteroids.**

elim: Lubricants alone undertreat active moderate-to-severe disease.
No infection is present.
Radioiodine would worsen active disease.
No optic neuropathy, so decompression is not first.

steps.x: **A. IV corticosteroids.** Active moderate-to-severe TED.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with thyroid eye disease has compressive optic neuropathy in her left eye. She has received high-dose IV methylprednisolone for 1 week. Her left acuity has fallen further from 6/18 to 6/60 and the left RAPD persists. CT orbits shows enlarged extraocular muscles crowding the orbital apex. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 140/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue IV steroids and review in 6 weeks
practice.e: Sight-threatening optic neuropathy failing IV steroids needs urgent orbital decompression to relieve pressure on the nerve. Thyroidectomy treats the gland, not the orbit.

steps.x: Next step after first-line emergency treatment has failed.
Vision worsening despite steroids, apex crowded on CT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent orbital decompression.**

elim: Waiting risks permanent blindness.
Lubricants protect the cornea, not the optic nerve.
Carbimazole does not decompress the orbit.
Thyroidectomy does not relieve orbital pressure.

steps.x: **E. Urgent orbital decompression surgery.** Steroids fail + RAPD = decompress.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman with Graves' disease has progressive bilateral proptosis over 6 months. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg. MRI of the orbits shows enlarged extraocular muscles and increased orbital fat.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her proptosis?
o: Infiltration of the orbit by lymphoma cells
practice.e: TSH receptor antibodies activate orbital fibroblasts, which proliferate and make glycosaminoglycans, swelling muscle and fat inside the fixed bony orbit. Sympathetic overactivity causes lid retraction, not true proptosis.

steps.x: Mechanism of a physical sign.

clues: enlarged extraocular muscles and increased orbital fat
steps.x: TRAb-driven expansion of orbital contents.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: TRAb stimulate **orbital fibroblasts** to make **glycosaminoglycans**, causing oedema.

elim: Haemorrhage is sudden and traumatic.
Raised ICP causes papilloedema, not proptosis.
Lymphoma is not antibody-driven or bilateral like this.
Müller's muscle overactivity explains lid retraction only.

steps.x: **A. Antibody-stimulated orbital fibroblasts.** Swelling in a fixed box pushes the eye forward.

prompts.q: What is thyroid eye disease, and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the tissue, the parent disease and the risk factors.

points.p: Autoimmune inflammation of the orbital tissues
points.why: Also called Graves' orbitopathy or thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy.
Graves' also links to type 1 diabetes and RA.

prompts.q: List the symptoms of thyroid eye disease.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: surface symptoms first, then pressure and movement symptoms.

points.why: Blurring with reduced acuity is a red flag.

points.p: Pressure behind the eye; prominent eyes

prompts.q: What are the named signs of thyroid eye disease?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match each eponym to what you would see.

points.p: Dalrymple's sign: lid retraction showing the superior limbus
points.why: Never visible in a normal eye.

points.p: Von Graefe's sign: lid lag on down gaze

points.why: Specific to Graves' rather than other thyrotoxic causes.

prompts.q: What are the complications and the red flags for sight-threatening disease?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: surface damage is common; optic nerve damage is the emergency.

points.p: Reduced visual acuity or colour vision
points.why: Colour loss is often first in optic neuropathy.

points.p: Optic disc changes or corneal ulceration

prompts.q: How is thyroid eye disease diagnosed, and when is imaging needed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: clinical plus TFTs; image only for red flags.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis, no single confirmatory test
TFTs first-line: low TSH, high T4
RAPD present: urgent CT or MRI orbits

points.why: Crowding at the orbital apex compresses the nerve.

prompts.q: How is mild thyroid eye disease managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three things for every patient.

points.p: Control the thyroid: carbimazole, beta-blocker, definitive treatment if needed

prompts.q: How is active moderate-to-severe and sight-threatening disease managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: step up by activity and severity, then go urgent for the optic nerve.

points.why: If vision fails to recover on IV steroids.

points.p: Avoid radioiodine in active disease (or give steroid cover)

prompts.q: Why does Graves' disease cause proptosis and diplopia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: antibody, cell, product, then the fixed bony box.

points.p: Orbital fibroblasts express the TSH receptor
points.why: Shared antigen with thyroid follicular cells.

points.p: TSH receptor antibodies (possibly IGF-1R) activate them
points.why: The same antibodies that cause thyrotoxicosis.

points.p: Fibroblasts proliferate and make glycosaminoglycans: oedema of muscle and fat
Fixed bony orbit pushes the eye forward and can compress the optic nerve
Diplopia: restrictive myopathy from fibrosis and oedema
points.why: Mechanical tethering, not a nerve palsy.

prompts.q: Why do smoking and radioactive iodine make thyroid eye disease worse?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one adds inflammation, the other adds antibody.

points.p: Smoking increases oxidative stress and cytokines
Radioiodine transiently raises TSH receptor antibodies

glossary.Thyroid eye disease: Autoimmune inflammation of the tissues around the eye, usually with Graves' disease.
glossary.Graves' orbitopathy: Another name for thyroid eye disease.
glossary.Graves' disease: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor.
glossary.Orbit: The bony socket that holds the eye, its muscles and fat.
glossary.Proptosis: Forward bulging of the eye out of the orbit.
glossary.Exophthalmos: Proptosis due to thyroid eye disease; the eye bulges forward.
glossary.Dalrymple's sign: Upper lid retraction so white sclera shows above the iris in straight-ahead gaze.
glossary.Von Graefe's sign: The upper eyelid lags behind the eye when looking down.
glossary.Lid lag: The upper lid is slow to follow the eye down; can occur in any thyrotoxicosis.
glossary.Lid retraction: The eyelid sits higher than normal, exposing sclera above the iris.
glossary.Superior limbus: The upper edge where the cornea meets the white sclera.
glossary.Photophobia: Discomfort or pain in the eyes caused by light.
glossary.Conjunctival injection: Redness of the white of the eye from dilated surface blood vessels.
glossary.Exposure keratopathy: Damage to the cornea from drying because the lids cannot cover it properly.
glossary.Lagophthalmos: Inability to close the eyelids fully.
glossary.RAPD: Relative afferent pupillary defect: the pupil dilates when a light swings to it, showing optic nerve damage.
glossary.Relative afferent pupillary defect: Abnormal swinging light test showing reduced signal from one optic nerve.
glossary.Compressive optic neuropathy: Optic nerve damage from swollen orbital contents pressing on it; sight-threatening.
glossary.Extraocular muscles: The six muscles that move each eye.
glossary.Inferior rectus: Eye muscle that pulls the eye down; often enlarged in TED, so upgaze is restricted.
glossary.Restrictive myopathy: Stiff, swollen muscle that cannot stretch, so the eye cannot move fully.
glossary.Orbital fibroblasts: Connective tissue cells in the orbit that carry the TSH receptor and drive swelling in TED.
glossary.Glycosaminoglycans: Water-attracting molecules made by fibroblasts that cause tissue swelling.
glossary.TRAb: TSH receptor antibodies, which cause Graves' disease and drive thyroid eye disease.
glossary.TSH receptor antibodies: Autoantibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor; diagnostic of Graves' disease.
glossary.IGF-1: Insulin-like growth factor 1; its receptor may also be targeted in thyroid eye disease.
glossary.Radioactive iodine: Radioiodine treatment that destroys thyroid tissue; can worsen eye disease.
glossary.Carbimazole: Antithyroid drug that blocks thyroid hormone synthesis.
glossary.Orbital decompression: Surgery removing orbital bone or fat to relieve pressure on the eye and optic nerve.
glossary.Methylprednisolone: Corticosteroid given IV for active moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease.
glossary.Clinical Activity Score: Seven-point score of pain, redness and swelling; 3 or more means active thyroid eye disease.
glossary.CAS: Clinical Activity Score for thyroid eye disease activity.
glossary.EUGOGO: European Group on Graves' Orbitopathy, which sets management principles for thyroid eye disease.
glossary.Hertel exophthalmometry: Measurement of how far the cornea sits in front of the lateral orbital rim.
glossary.Fluorescein: Orange dye that stains damaged corneal surface green under blue light.
glossary.Swinging light test: Moving a torch between the eyes to detect a relative afferent pupillary defect.
glossary.Orbital apex: The back of the orbit where muscles converge around the optic nerve.
